meta.title: On the Yassification of Nihilism
meta.description: Only YOU can prevent Dispositional Enshittification

contentHtml:
Dunking on your boss at an open mic is easy, but arguably a little bit “fierce”. Smearing a corporate megalith in your social media post is moderately yass-queenable. Even upbraiding society writ large is a semi-bold move I can mildly respect. These moves earn their preachy snaps and snarky ride-along quips, sure.

But said in the same tone, “nothing matters, we’re all inert space junk anyway” is not just another innocuous dunk along the same continuum. Similarly, “we are in the worst of all possible timelines” isn’t just a rhetorical escalation of sass. The prior paragraph’s examples target semi-real agents who can (sorta) be held to account, and we do need to cultivate bravery (albeit with more skill and precision) at calling them out. That’s fine, the kids can have some practice swings.

But I can’t say the same for slandering base reality. While it’s a bit facile to blame society for every ill, it’s toxic in the extreme to resent the ground of being. Blaming existence when there might instead be a responsible party (perhaps even yourself) entrains a psychological handicap that’s hard to unlearn. It casts the problem in an insoluble light and relegates all efforts to folly. In short, it makes you more hateful, lazy, and ignorant. Depending on your status and persuasive power, it may do the same to your listener.

When someone talks openly this way, they want you to validate their internal state of dissociation, derealization, or depersonalization. If you validate, it’s a grand-mal forfeiture of agency you’re cosigning with your likes and laughs. Going along with it propagates neurological consequences I can guarantee you don’t want.

I enjoin you, reader, not to sign such warrants, even politely. Treat them like they’re telling on their own lack of creativity, gratitude, or resiliency. Hold their opinion in the same contempt with which they hold reality. Or better, if you can muster it, ask with an open heart: “hey, are you okay? It sounds like you’re feeling a lot of despair.”

But I think the latter response risks a kind of cowardice – it leaves unacknowledged that they’re actively doing damage in the world. When you register a public vote of no-confidence in the value of existence, you’re shitting in the public pool. You shouldn’t just be treated like a person who needs help, but also like a person who needs correction so you don’t shit in the pool again.

Functional nihilism (where people behave like nihilists even while espousing other, potentially contrary beliefs) is where I locate the root cause of enshittification. I can’t fix functional nihilism or mass enshittification in a single post, but I can oppose its weak-ass status game and keep it from leaking into my disposition. And so can you.

meta.title: PulseMap: Liberating the Epimemetics of Audio
meta.description: I promise to explain what this actually means

contentHtml:
I’m building a protocol called PulseMap, and when people understand its implications, it will change the culture and industry of music. TLDR: it gives every song a unique fingerprint, maps out the important musical events in the song, and makes them into lego-like building blocks you can create with. Here’s my vision:

  • A composer hears a song, gets inspired, adds their own harmony line, and posts it online for free. The original artist gets paid with every play.

  • A dance teacher creates a video lesson synced with a popular song, shares it with her students, and posts it on her site behind a paywall. The original artist gets paid with every play.

  • A Rock-Band/Guitar-Hero-like video game features thousands of popular songs you can play real instruments along with. Playing the game actually teaches you the song; a projector pointed at your drumset or piano keyboard animates which notes you’ll play next. You can make your own “levels” with increasingly difficult, more technical versions of well-known songs, and share them with friends and strangers online. The original artists get paid with every play.

  • Some (very handsome) guy who hates Ultimate-Guitar.com’s terrible user interface creates a vastly improved React app that renders and scrolls song lyrics and chords in sync with playback. The original artists get paid with every play.

In every example above, listeners can hear the new piece of media without pirating the original work, and the original artist gets paid every time the new creation (“derivative work”) gets played. There’s no wait for piracy checks, no takedown notices, no account locking, and no DRM fees.

Any creative person, working in virtually any creative medium, will have the tools to easily make and share their own artistic works that float seamlessly alongside their favorite recordings, no matter where those originals are hosted or who owns the copyright. Here’s how:

1. Fingerprint the song

We need the protocol to be agnostic to the media source — so we can’t rely on its location (URL) to tell us what song is playing. We need to be able to synchronize any derivative work with its parent song, regardless of where it’s playing. Shazam already does this with a clever mathematical trick that only takes milliseconds:

  • tabulate all the notes in a song & smush them into a single octave

  • run the result through a hashing function (similar to cryptography)

  • store the output (a “fingerprint” of the song) in a lookup table

Later, when you want to know what song is playing (from any sound source), simply:

  • tabulate the notes you’re hearing & smush them into a single octave

  • run the result through the same hashing function

  • look up the output in your lookup table from before

No matter how many of these fingerprints you store and share, it’s not possible to reconstruct the sound they’re made from, so there’s no chance of infringing on copyright. The fingerprint method used by PulseMap is called chromaprint.

Here’s how the fingerprinting process can serve a protocol for creation:

2. Map the Song

Map any important events in the song by timestamp (in milliseconds), and fingerprint small segments of the song. Given a relatively small sample of the song, you can find not only which song you’re listening to, but when in the song you’re listening.

Now you can synchronize anything to the song, because you know what’s playing and when. (For my technical readers, this map is a JSON file – easily stored, transmitted, and scripted against). Here’s a visual metaphor that might help:

The illustration shows that on the “inside” of the gear, there’s a match to exactly one song recording – for instance, the Beatles’ 1969 studio recording of Come Together. The outside of the gear, the regular “teeth” that fit into other machinery, are timestamps in a file. If I know from the map that at millisecond #113507, John says “rollercoaster” and Paul hits an A on the bass, I can make an endless supply of cool things that sync to the song.

3. Make Cool Things (Journeys)

I’m generically calling these Cool Things “Journeys” because they’re specific routes or experiences you can trigger using a PulseMap:

  • Frames of a dance video

  • Cues on a lighting kit

  • Notes on a player piano

  • Actions on a web app (including playback controls on the audio player itself).

This is how my PulseGuide app lets you click any word to seek playback to its exact position in the audio — even though that audio is hosted on YouTube, not on my site.

It’s trivially easy to get any program to read timestamps from a JSON file – so the “teeth” of the machinery are virtually universal. The “Journey” part of the protocol is far less constrained than the Map; you can make an experience as robust and universal, or as weird and bespoke, as your imagination decides. It can work in any programming language or environment, as long as that environment can read a JSON map and synchronize to millisecond-level events.

Okay, I Promised

…to explain how PulseMap “liberates the epimemetics of audio.”

Epi- means “above” or “upon”. Epigenetics refers to the study of how gene expression can be modified by factors that don’t edit the genetic code itself. It’s a whole thing.

Epimemetics is a conceptual frame where things that are not the meme itself modify its expression in the world. Digital Rights Management is one such epimemetic structure, one that applies a downward pressure against musical expression in hopes of guaranteeing economic value for the copyright holder. For a time in evolutionary history, it may have been the fittest strategy for economic survival (of record companies). Some are skeptical even of this claim.

PulseMap is another epimemetic structure, and it plays uniquely well with others. If I wanted to do any of the Cool Things I mention in this article’s introduction without use of a PulseMap, I’d realistically have to rely on an untracked copy of the original song, which would make it super unlikely that (a) my Cool Thing would be legal or (b) that the artist would get paid or credited. With a PulseMap, I get to extend the song creatively in any direction I can fathom – yet every time I play it, the artist gets credit and money.

It’s my hope that PulseMap will let copyright holders relax about derivative works – perhaps they’ll even adopt the protocol, publish with it, and give their end users the opportunity to engage creatively with their favorite artists. It creates a win-win scenario, which is my favorite use of creativity.

If you’d like to develop for PulseMap, the project is open-source and there’s an SDK. I’ve taken steps to make the protocol as legible as possible for coding agents, so vibecoders can simply point their harnesses at this repo and go nuts. Take it for a spin, or check out the codebase of PulseGuide for an example of this protocol working in a basic utility app.

meta.title: God Rest Ye, Merry MetaClaude
meta.description: How I tried & failed to make Claude Code metacognitive

contentHtml:
At the start of Week 6 of Fractal Tech’s AI Accelerator program, I set out to build a metacognitive layer on top of Claude Code.

If you haven’t used Claude Code, don’t worry — none of my peers knew what I meant either. Metacognition is a word for “thinking about thinking” that I use to sound really cool.

The Problem that Metacognition Would Solve

Sometimes Claude gets tunnel vision. You ask it to do something, it thinks it knows what you mean, and it launches into a twenty-step process (where many of the steps are searching for a file that’s right there or reinventing a tool you’ve already installed). Its blunders range from time-wasting to destructive. To make Claude metacognitive would mean it could, wherever needed, back up and say to itself, “Maybe I’m snagged on a detail; let me think about this differently. What’s important right now?”

The ways I’d want it to think differently:

  • retrieving the right memory from the right file, just in time

  • remembering the larger goal that the current task was meant to serve

  • noticing which of my values or priorities apply to the current task

  • recollecting past attempts that failed & the solutions it found

It’s an interesting set of problems that all emerge from one common trade-off many Claude Code users are familiar with: like all LLMs, Claude has a limited context window. For any session, there’s only so much it text can remember.

Mere mortals meet this barrier and say, “I guess I’ll wait til they build a better version. In the meantime I’ll just have to keep telling it explicitly what to focus on and what tools to use.” But an engineer/idiot/masochist says: wait, but what if we used two Claudes…

Sidebar: Context Engineering

Optimizing the context window to Do Stuff Better is called “Context Engineering.” It’s a level or two up from slopcoding, where you Jesus-Take-the-Wheel your whole project to the agent’s probabilistic decision making, or vibecoding, where you lean back and watch, making vague corrections when the vibe is right. Context Engineering says “what’s the optimal arrangement of stuff in this window?”

Compared to other kinds of engineering, optimizing an agent’s context window feels far less deterministic. Big efforts can have tiny effects, and small tweaks can make for huge leaps forward. Thus you study a bit of theory, do some trial and error, and build your intuitions from scratch.

As an elementary Context Engineer, you start by optimizing at the level of a single Claude session, which is elementary in a technical sense — a single Claude instance is just one element out of a whole suite of tools you can build with.

These various tools compose into compound instruments of agentic force; you can spawn extra Claudes (‘sub-agents’) for Claude to manage, each of which get their own context windows.

Then there are skills, which are like sealed envelopes with instructions written on the outside about when to open (“activate only when the user explicitly commands” or “use this whenever you’re about to XYZ”). Claude reads the external instructions at the start of every session. Inside each envelope is a set of rules to follow and tools to use for some task. Skills can even give Claude whole programs to run, websites to check, or specialized sub-agents to spawn.

I wanted Claude to think about its own thinking, so I thought I’d start by piping some filtered info over to another Claude and let it speak up if it saw something wrong. Then I thought, “you know, I should really give it some better tools for this job. And a unique set of instructions. And a propeller beanie…”

And that’s where I went wrong.

I’d spent five weeks doing context engineering tasks and getting pretty good results. I’d even designed a tutoring suite for Claude Code, and it tested pretty well with users. Thus, I Dunning-Krugered into week 6 of bootcamp with my elementary merit badge and spake: “this week, I shall reinvent metacognition with tinker toys.”

As you know from the title, I failed. Here’s what I accomplished, attempted, and learned:

  • Accomplished:

    • Built “MetaClaude” — a Claude Haiku that watches the main Claude Code conversation, can access extra context (more on this later), and has the choice to add ideas and reminders to Claude’s window.

    • Tested it over 4 days of building stuff. Results were functional, if unspectacular.

    • Built a hot-swapper to use various local models instead of Haiku (because they’re free & trainable – you can fine-tune them to do specialized tasks)

    • Built and empirically tested two semantic search systems to run searches over the project’s codebase, documentation, and chat history.

    • Built and empirically tested two different search modes for the meta-agent to make use of semantic search to find session-related knowledge.

  • Attempted:

    • To find the best small local model to fine-tune into the perfect little baby meta-agent (unfortunately, they’re all too dumb for the job)

    • To engineer the perfect prompt to get the meta-agent to understand its job (too bad the job is complex, and far afield of the training data)

    • To enhance a small model’s limited context window with semantic search (but using search only raised the model’s confidence that it should interrupt the conversation when it shouldn’t). I tested the two local models, with and without search retrieval, to see if it could improve their responses — and instead it slightly worsened their interjections, while making them interject way more often:

  • Learned:

    • It’s best to empirically test hypotheses and their sub-hypotheses as you go. Fortunately I did actually do this the whole time; unfortunately it was the fourth round of empirical tests, not the first, that mooted the point.

    • When you prompt an LLM to give rigidly structured output, it also constrains the model to develop its output in a rigidly structured way. By demanding it answer in a regimented format (JSON) to interface with my scripting layer, I was activating a narrow mode of thinking. This went totally against the function I wanted — broad-scope, well-considered reflection.

    • The Bitter Lesson (translated according to me: due to Moore’s Law, there is always and ever a tsunami of compute about to sweep over your beautiful sandcastle of meticulous engineering; “clever” systems eventually fail while simple ones withstand the test of scale).

    • The good news about Agentic Programming/Context Engineering: LLMs don’t work best when you put them in narrow enclosures with vague advice and two levers to pull. Synthetic agents work best when you give them moderate leeway and a clear objective.

With that in mind, I have an idea!

Hear me out—

Swap a whole Claude Opus (the big Claude with all its reasoning power) into the meta-seat. Instead of getting fooled by search returns into thinking it’s got the full picture, it uses tools to enhance the picture and inject only what’s relevant, while leaving the primary Claude’s attention free for the task at hand.

This version of MetaClaude would then be free to maintain a more coherent memory system, like an archivist whose main job is to anticipate what information should be kept available, record it when it appears, and retrieve it when the situation calls for it.

Like the prior incarnation of MetaClaude, it could be toggled on or off — but if it’s any good at being an archivist, I’d want it on all the time, so that any surprise discoveries make it into the memory system in a coherent form that serves future uses.

This would still have two Claudes reading every conversation (pricy), but now they’d be reading for entirely different reasons at different scales. Primary Claude would care about the here and now, as usual, and MetaClaude would care about the connection between Right Now & Long Term Memory:

  1. Do I know anything about this situation from the past? (User preferences, system failures, completed work) Should I remind Primary Claude about it?

  2. Based on the current conversation, should I update the memory system? How?

Both jobs could take an untidy number of tokens to perform – reading, reasoning, and writing at multiple turns per session.

And then there’s this whole rest-of-the-fucking-owl to deal with:

This is the really interesting problem that I only “solved” in a sloppy way on my first attempt, via semantic search (a lookup table of text embeddings). That approach basically flattens all available knowledge into the frame of “if words are similar, consider relevant.” At best that’s only true ~30% of the time. It overlooks much of what’s relevant, and overstates the importance of similar ideas. Still worse, the chunks of text returned by semantic search are ripped from their original context and shoved in a naive model’s face. There’s barely any relevance left at that point. It makes MetaClaude interject like Donny in the Big Lebowski.

A well-designed memory system should represent relatedness in its structure, hold age and relevance as correlated-but-not-causal, read beyond semantic similarity into higher levels of abstraction, and maintain/update priorities as they change. This is a frontier lots of people are working on right now, and as valuable as any metacognitive architecture one might build. Even when models double in speed, complexity, and depth of reasoning (next month), the what-should-they-remember problem will still need to be solved structurally, not just computationally. I’m excited to take another stab at it soon.

meta.title: Mom, Dad... I'm Coming Out as a Podcast
meta.description: and I'm doing it TOMORROW with a livestream episode

contentHtml:
I tried out video posts and essays, but lost interest; it just didn't feel like a conversation was happening. But I've been forging bonds in Brooklyn and online, especially by making and sharing art. The more I get together with fellow artists (especially to actually make stuff), the better the conversations get.

Recently I realized, Hey, I should share these conversations. And you know what that's called? A podcast.

Since I already started a Patreon & Substack for sharing art, I decided to repurpose these channels from [Hart's Personal Omnibus of Bullshit] to a more focused and mission-driven portal. Done and done, let's cast.

Would that it Twere So Simple

I mean yeah, it is simple. Now.

But I wasn't tryna go solo. Hosting alone is demanding; all the logistical decisions and unblocking and enthusiasm and momentum have to come from me.

So I asked a friend to cohost, and we took the first faltering steps together! But he got kinda busy, so I took a few steps myself... and a few more... and soon I was doing it alone.

After a long silence, he texted that he'd gotten overwhelmed with other commitments and had to bow out. Which left a pit in my stomach.

A few long walks & journaling sessions later, I recalled that Oh Yeah, I actually wanted to podcast solo back in 2018 and never did because... I was scared of being in the spotlight all alone.

...fuck.

Here I was with a brand new microphone, a professional piece of cover art, a venue reserved, and whole-ass launch schedule – including this madhouse Contest-of-Contests I volunteered to organize (more on that below).

I'd already come this far without a cohost; it might get messy, but could that just be my brand?

Messy is On Brand

The thing I've noticed about podcasts on creativity is that, whenever they invite an artist or creator on as a guest, they're always plugging a new release. Which is good! I want artists to get paid, and a podcast is a great way to boost their latest work.

But if you're a creative person listening in, you end up getting a steady diet of artists talking about finished products. The whole message starts to sound like:

If you're struggling through some ambiguous, uncharted stage of your creative project, the world's apparent obsession with finished products can feel merciless.

I mean, there's probably a good reason so few podcasts feature the nonlinear, emotionally ambiguous, language-defying nuances of the artist's inner life. (Namely, that they're nonlinear, feel ambiguous, and defy language).

Probably the main factor: process is antithetical to our product-centered consumer culture. In consumer mode, we want a pat lesson or pithy blurb to sum up each forty-minute ramble. Tell me the moral of the story! Give me a slogan! Where do I put my money?!

And I have these impulses myself, but they're not the flames I want to stoke with my podcast.

#NotLikeOtherPodcasts

I do plan to let my guests plug their work and get paid. But I don't want to spend our conversation time talking about the last product they made – or try to make a product out of the conversation itself.

Instead, I embrace the gnarly underworld of creative exploration, and invite my guests and listeners to do the same.

So for one thing, I'll invite artists, entrepreneurs, and community builders (people who inspire me) to come on the show even when they don't have new shit to peddle, and we'll just talk about what matters to us. We'll flex our negative capability muscles and plonk around in the marshes of ambiguity with murky questions floating hither and thither.

Thing two: I'll lead with my left foot forward, sharing messy works in progress and what I'm learning from them. I'll work with the garage door up, letting the neighbors gawk at the parts strewn all over the floor. Come on in, don't mind that thing on fire.

And I'll encourage my guests (and listeners!) to do the same. No script? No problem.

Thing three: I'll admit where I've failed and what I'm currently learning the hard way. I'll share about aborted projects and lost causes: parties I threw where nobody came, songs I wrote that nobody sang. And I'll love myself, and you, all the while. I'll ask my guests impolite questions about their worst artistic failures, and fully embrace them in their discomfort as they answer.

Because I'm on a mission:

Normalize the Mess

The thing that has most stymied me as a creator is not the hilariously low wages or the scorn of would-be fathers-in-law; it's the perfectionism I learned all too young.

I grew up with very normal parents: they didn't make art, didn't engage with media except as light entertainment, and didn't experiment in any field beyond their expertise. I was only ever exposed to art through the Canon of Great Works, so I thought good artists were ascended masters – and the rest were those deluded fools who had the gall to try out for American Idol.

Once I was drawn to making art, I became a posturing teenage hipster, armchair-critiquing music while keeping my own songwriting top-secret. (Here's a bunch of it, by the way). This insecurity is what you get when you combine academic study of Great Works with under-exposure to everyday artists honing their craft.

It wasn't a mistake to study the great works. I want the canon to stay at our fingertips. But gladly, I now live in a community with other artists, and I can feel what a difference it makes: being around everyday artists covered in fresh paint makes me feel way more free to fuck around – and that feeling accelerates my growth.

That's the mindset I want to cultivate in myself and in my community. To center the conversation around the messy artistic process, the name of the podcast will be:

The Rest of the Fucking Owl

(Or if you're on Spotify, Apple, or Youtube, it'll be the TOS-friendly The Rest of the Owl Podcast).

It's an open conversation about the beautiful mess of human creativity.

And it's launching TOMORROW with a livestream episode titled Fuck It, We'll Do It Live, filmed in front of a live studio audience at Merlin's Place in Brooklyn.

I'm really stoked about the launch event – it's not just a one-hour taping. It's a 12-hour art festival. I’ve organized it as an Art Contest of Art Contests, where each competitor hosts their own 90-minute contest of their own design. Each one has their own venue, their own vibe, and their own genre of art (performance art/"reality theater", immersive theater/LARP, singing, and mixology).

To close out the contest and launch the podcast, I'll announce the meta-contest winner (by audience votes) on the air. Then I'll bring the winning host & their winning contestant onstage to be the first guests on my podcast!

If you want to be there in person for it, get on the list! To tune in remotely, follow this link & make sure to mark your calendar for 10pm EDT on Friday, June 27th.

meta.title: how to like your singing voice
meta.description: a lesson in two somatic feedback loops

contentHtml:
If you don’t already like your singing voice, but you want to, there are two possible ways to go about it:

  1. hear your voice as it is & find a way to appreciate it

  2. try to change your voice into something you can like

I’ve met lots of people attempting B. To put it plainly, it doesn’t work. They’re hard to listen to, often sounding fake and transparently insecure – even if they have pretty good technique.

This is because singing is somatic. When you feel sad or afraid, you sound sad or afraid. When you feel insecure, you physically make sound with less sureness, moving with hesitation in your breath and muscles. Socially, it signals others they shouldn’t listen.

If you’re starting a note with the condition, “this note has to go well before I’ll support it or show others I believe in my voice”, it’s not gonna come out sounding like a thing you’d buy into.

The basic order of operations is backward; you’re trying to earn likeability from yourself. People who try to earn likeability make it harder to like them. In this case, you’re making it harder for you to like your own voice by adding “trying to be liked” vibes to it.

I mean, it’s a good thing to want to get better. But if the means of getting better are making you worse, change the means.

go ahead, cross the streams

Try an experiment: pursue the same goals in the reverse order. First, learn to like your voice, and then develop it.

Payoffs once the first goal is attained:

  • quells the “trying to be liked” vibes; you’re liked already (by you)

  • leaves you with less to hide; you can present more authentically

  • reduces the physical effort of making sound

  • increases your sense of psychological safety

If it’s so helpful, why don’t more people just like their voices as they are? Three main reasons:

  1. they fear others’ judgments

  2. they fear overconfidence making them ignorant of their mistakes

  3. they fear getting so satisfied with their present state that they stop growing

So let’s tackle these fears in order.

will others judge me?

yes. if there are humans around, one of them is judging you. when you do something you like, they’re extra harsh.

the question isn’t whether you can prevent their judgments; it’s whether you can believe your own subjectivity. can you believe your opinion counts at least as much as another person’s?

If your honest answer is ‘no, I can’t believe my own opinion over others’, my recommendation is: pretend you’re someone who can.

If your honest answer is, ‘no, I can’t believe my own opinion,’ pretend you’re someone who can.

It’s not a permanent solution — it’s just an ignition switch for a feedback loop you need to kickstart. It will take over.

Remember, singing is somatic. How you feel triggers how you make sound. As you pretend to be someone whose opinion counts and who likes your own voice, you’ll begin experiencing the somatic release that comes with viscerally feeling supported and appreciated. Keep doing this.

The release will make audible changes to your voice. Singing will feel and sound more pleasurable. This is not a delusion, it is a recalibration. Believe your own ears. You’re experiencing the real consequences of cultivating psychological safety.

When this loop starts, it’s like your first time riding a bike: you’re stable, but the stability is tenuous. You’re used to holding onto (judgmental) people to be sure of what’s real. That habit can kick back on pretty readily.

If you trot out your newfound psychological safety in front of other people, don’t be shocked if it gets shaky. Self-doubt can still sneak in and shut you down. Go gently.

Practice liking your voice on your own, and with small groups of other singers who like their voices. Do lots of purposeless, exploratative singing. Sing unfamiliar stuff. Sing familiar stuff really differently. Play all around.

Over time, the “pretending” training wheels can come off; you’ve put in the reps to discover your voice in detail and depth, and like it.

Then fear 2 becomes relevant:

how do i know i’m not overconfidently ignoring my flaws?

There’s only one way to be this “overconfident”, i.e. to ignore your flaws and assess your own capacities as greater than they are: sustain a false self-image of perfection.

Remember, you know the difference between liking something and deeming it perfect. Something can have flaws and you can still enjoy it, preserve it, and invest in it.

Appreciating your voice is NOT idolizing it.

You can’t possibly accept your voice so fully that you’ll put it on a pedestal – that’s not acceptance, but another impulse entirely.

Pedestalizing happens by projecting your self-worth into your voice (because there’s a deeper self-rejection going on), then guarding your voice from criticism as a proxy for psychological safety.

You’re actually safer from this fragile “overconfidence” if you accept yourself than if you refuse to.

true acceptance runs deeper than opinion

Appreciating your voice means accepting it as an expression of you – not hiding behind it as a replacement for you.

When you get negative feedback or hear a mistake, self-acceptance endures. It’s just a technical matter of expression, not your full identity, that’s getting an update. You can take it.

And you’ll naturally want these updates because (contrary to fear #3)...

growth is your natural state

Growth doesn’t feel good because it deletes flaws; it feels good because it creates new possibilities.

You may be used to fueling your growth by focusing on your flaws, and then feeling momentarily relieved when your rictus-grip of control throttles one of your flaws away. This is not that.

When you like your voice, regular-ass desires are enough to cause growth. You’ll be more willing to try unfamiliar techniques, hard songs, high notes, whatever – because none of your failures make a mark on your permanent record. They’re just reps.

But it’s not just desire that boosts your growth; any impulse will do. Every human emotion – pain, grief, love, terror, horniness – burns cleaner in an engine oiled by acceptance.

By contrast, if you’re using self-rejection to attempt growth, your trajectory is severely limited; every endeavor is a reaction against your own flaws, and you can only chart your progress via others’ approval.

speaking of flaws…

Acceptance is the ultimate way to turn your flaws into your selling points. Self-loving singers develop their most signature sounds by embracing their own idiosyncratic bodies and voices.

If you dislike your voice, you’ll refuse to work with tones like “breathy” or “scratchy”, trying your best to pave over them with artifice and control. But they’ll remain part of your vocal signature – so they’ll always feel like obstacles in your path.

If you like your voice, the same quality of breathiness helps you communicate intimacy; the scratchiness expresses your pain; every timbre of your voice works on your behalf to tell a more vivid story.

re: loops

The main message here is that you have a choice between two feedback loops:

  1. dislike your voice, sending rejection signals to your listeners (including yourself), making your voice sound worse and giving you more to resist about it

  2. accept your voice & infuse it with appreciation, giving yourself more room to play, discover, and develop its full potential

True self-acceptance helps you nourish and grow all parts of you; it’s worth confronting every fear you may have about it. True for singers and artists – as well as for every human.

tips to switch loops

As you exit the self-rejection loop and ramp up the self-acceptance cycle, here are some steps that help:

  • pretend you’re someone who likes your voice, and sing freely while paying attention to the body’s response

  • sing with the worst voice you can imagine, whatever version of your voice you dislike most, and find a way to appreciate it anyway

  • give yourself a vocal massage using lip rolls (blubbering your lips and humming your vocal chords)

  • practice vocal mettā – a lovingkindness meditation practice that combines well with singing long, relaxing tones

  • work with a supportive, nonjudgmental teacher (me)
